c.v: Wood shake roofing

runs.v: covers a sloped roof in hand-split or tapersawn wood shakes, most often western red cedar, laid over a ventilated assembly that lets each course dry from the underside after rainfall. The air space beneath the shakes manages the moisture that drives most cedar wear. Wood shake is the broader category — thick split shakes, thinner sawn wood shingles, and several species of natural wood — and anyone comparing wood shake roofing Newark NJ options is weighing the rustic charm of a real wood roof against three practical questions: the grade of the wood, its fire rating under New Jersey's building code, and the maintenance it will need for decades.

Humidity in NJ significantly affects cedar roof lifespan, and summer humidity plus winter freeze-thaw are the harsh weather conditions a wood roof in Newark has to shed, so the air space gives every exposed course protection from trapped moisture.

sections.heading: Wood Shakes vs. Wood Shingles: Species and Grades

c.v: Wood shakes are thicker and split on at least one face for a rough, textured surface, while wood shingles are machine-sawn on both sides for a smooth, uniform surface.

runs.v: Hand-split and resawn shakes cast the deepest shadow lines and the most rustic look, tapersawn shakes are sawn on both faces for a classic look between a shake and a shingle, and sawn shingles lie flatter and tighter on the roof. Western red cedar is the standard species because its natural oils resist decay and insects and it stays dimensionally stable through wet-dry cycles; Alaskan yellow cedar is denser and weathers to a silver-gray; eastern white cedar is milled mostly into shingles; and pressure-treated southern yellow pine tapersawn shakes rely on the treatment rather than natural oils for decay resistance. Premium grade cedar — clear, all-heartwood, edge-grain stock — is essential for longevity in a humid climate like New Jersey's, because flat-grain pieces cup and split sooner and sapwood decays faster, and New Jersey's residential code specifies grading requirements for wood shakes, with cedar graded under Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau rules.

sections.heading: Fire Risk and Code Rules for Wood Shake Roofs in Newark

c.v: Fire risk is the first code question for any wood roof, because untreated wood has a higher vulnerability to fire: untreated wood shakes are nonclassified under UL 790 and ASTM E108.

runs.v: Pressure-impregnated fire-retardant treatment gives shakes a Class B or Class C rating, and a Class A wood roof is reached only as an assembly of Class B fire-retardant shakes over a fire-retardant cap sheet. Municipal codes may require Class A or B fire-rated materials in densely populated areas; New Jersey sets one statewide Uniform Construction Code that follows the International Residential Code (IRC) for one- and two-family homes, and the IRC requires a Class A, B, or C roof covering wherever the roof edge sits less than 3 feet from a lot line, a condition common on narrow city lots. The same code regulates wood shake installation and compliance beyond fire: it specifies grading requirements, requires corrosion-resistant fasteners, and on a permitted re-roof bars a recover over existing wood shake, so a wood shake roof may need to be removed before a new roof covering is installed.

c.v: Historic districts pull the other way.

runs.v: Cedar shake roofing has been used since the colonial era, cedar shake is preferred in historic districts for authenticity, and cedar shake roofs are often required in historic districts where the original roof was wood. Essex County towns such as Glen Ridge and South Orange, like Newark's Forest Hill, include designated historic districts, where a change of roofing material on a historic property can require review by the local historic preservation commission, which is why cedar remains the go-to choice for historic NJ homes and a synthetic look-alike is not always accepted.

sections.heading: Wood Shake vs. Asphalt Shingles and Other Roofing Materials

c.v: Wood shake roofing trades a higher price and more maintenance for natural beauty, insulation, and a classic look that asphalt shingles cannot match.

runs.v: Cedar shake roofs require more maintenance than traditional roofing materials — annual cleaning to prevent moss growth, clearing debris, and preservative or chemical treatment every 3 to 5 years — while asphalt shingles typically last 20 to 30 years with little or no maintenance. Wood is good insulation: cedar provides roughly double the insulation value of asphalt shingles, so wood shakes offer superior thermal insulation that helps keep an attic cooler in summer and warm in winter, trimming cooling costs and improving energy efficiency. Wood shakes can withstand heavy winds and severe storms when properly maintained, so their durability tracks the upkeep; with proper maintenance, cedar shake roofs can last 30 to 50 years, and wood is a renewable, natural material that is biodegradable at the end of its lifespan. In Newark, wood shake roofing offers strong curb appeal and natural insulation but requires higher maintenance than other materials, and some New Jersey roofing guides estimate that a cedar roof adds 5 to 7% to a home's value in Essex County, a figure to treat as an estimate rather than an appraisal rule.

c.v: Where the fire rules or the upkeep rule out real wood, synthetic shake, metal, and architectural asphalt are the usual alternatives.

runs.v: Synthetic (composite) shakes mold a shake profile from polymer, and many carry a Class A fire rating; metal shake-profile and standing-seam panels last for decades; and architectural asphalt such as GAF Timberline HDZ, which Newark Quality Roofing installs, costs the least up front. Real cedar remains the right choice when a historic district requires wood or the owner wants the natural wood appearance that only real shakes give. Converting from cedar to asphalt means tearing off to the deck and adding solid plywood sheathing, because shakes are often laid over spaced boards that asphalt shingles cannot span.

faqs.q: How long does a wood shake roof last in the New Jersey climate?

runs.v: With proper maintenance, cedar shakes can last 20 to 40 years and cedar shingles 30 to 50 years, per the Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau, against the single 25-year "Wood" figure on the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart. Humidity in NJ accelerates decay of cedar shake roofs, and without maintenance a cedar roof often lasts only 15 to 20 years.

faqs.q: Are wood shake roofs a fire hazard?

runs.v: Untreated wood shakes are nonclassified for fire under UL 790 and ASTM E108, while pressure-impregnated fire-retardant shakes carry a Class B or Class C rating. A Class A wood roof is reached only as an assembly of Class B fire-retardant shakes over a fire-retardant cap sheet.

faqs.q: What maintenance does a wood shake roof require?

runs.v: Wood shake maintenance clears moss and debris every year, applies a fungicide, algaecide, or preservative treatment every 3 to 5 years, and replaces individual cupped or split shakes before the damage spreads. Treatment costs $0.15 to $0.60 per square foot per cycle, per HomeGuide cost data, and staying on schedule can save a cedar roof from early replacement.

faqs.q: What is the difference between wood shakes and wood shingles?

runs.v: Wood shakes are thicker and split or tapersawn for a rough, textured surface; wood shingles are machine-sawn on both sides for a smooth, uniform surface. Shakes give the more rustic look, while shingles lie flatter.

faqs.q: How do you know when to repair or replace a wood shake roof?

runs.v: Replace a wood shake roof when more than 25 to 30% of the shakes cup or split, or when a shake cracks under the light-bending flex test. Below that threshold, individual shake replacement and flashing repair usually keep the roof in service.

faqs.q: How much does wood shake roofing cost in Essex County, NJ?

runs.v: Wood shake repair averages roughly $750 nationally, with a range of $400 to $1,800, and replacing shakes runs about $600 to $700 per 100-square-foot square. New Jersey ranges sit roughly 10 to 40% above national figures, and a cedar install lands at $10 to $20-plus per square foot here.

faqs.q: Does a wood shake roof in Newark require a permit?

runs.v: Repair or replacement of the cedar roof covering on a detached one- or two-family home counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires no construction permit. A commercial cedar roof repair covering more than 25% of the roof area in 12 months does require a permit.

faqs.q: What are the common problems with wood shake roofs?

runs.v: Most wood shake problems trace to moisture: moss, mold, and mildew growth, rot on shaded slopes, and shakes that cup, split, or curl as they wet and dry. Termites and other insects are rarely the cause, but untreated wood carries a higher fire risk, and every wood roof needs more maintenance than asphalt.
